newsitem.title: UK: IEA sees non-OPEC oil racing ahead after delays.
newsitem.headline: IEA sees non-OPEC oil racing ahead after delays.

text.p: Non-OPEC oil supplies should race ahead this year after delays and technical snags put a cap on expected new flows in 1996, the International Energy Agency (IEA) said on Tuesday.
The IEA sees non-OPEC production rising two million barrels a day (bpd) this year to 45.6 million and said the supply disruptions of last year were not likely to be repeated.

"If analysed in detail, the lower-than-anticipated non-OPEC production...in almost all cases is the result of temporary factors that are not likely to be repeated in 1997," the agency said in a monthly oil market report.

As delayed fields are brought on stream in the first half of 1997 and performance at older fields begins to benefit from new technologies, "greater credibility should start to be given to the more aggressive supply scenarios," it said.
Lessons learned in new producing areas, such as the West of Shetland Foinaven field, would reduce the chance of further delays.
The agency said both the geological case and the economic base for new oil projects remained favourable.
"The evidence strongly indicates that neither the perceived geological nor the economic bases for oil projects worsened in 1996."
The IEA said it expected the North Sea to lead the rise in supply this year by pumping an extra 800,000 bpd.
It said 19 new British oilfields were scheduled to start production this year after 17 came on stream in 1996 adding 495,000 bpd to UK output.
Seven new Norwegian fields would provide an extra 278,000 bpd.
Latin American producers were expected to contribute an extra 510,000 bpd with almost half the increase from Brazil where several large offshore projects are due on stream.
Mexico should increase oil flows by 115,000 bpd, Colombian output is seen rising 85,000 bpd and Argentina should add 50,00 bpd, the IEA said.
Non-OPEC African supply is expected to rise 250,000 bpd led by an extra 100,000 bpd from Angola and an 85,000 bpd rise from Congo.
